lead.headline: Trump says the US has struck Iran's Qeshm Island again, calling it 'minor', as Washington offers $20m for nuclear secrets
lead.short: Donald Trump said on Friday that the US had carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, hitting an air defence system on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. "They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," he said.

why.text: Every strike in Hormuz threatens the talks that have pushed oil below $100, and with it India's fuel bill.

more: They are the first US strikes since Tuesday's midterm defeat, which voters' anger over the war and fuel prices helped bring about. The US military had already carried out what it called "defensive" strikes on Monday on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and near Bandar Abbas. Since the election Trump has swung between threatening to "destroy" Iran and saying a deal is near.

US Central Command offered on Friday "a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran's nuclear program", including its facilities and scientists. Trump said mediators' talks with Iran continue, and Gulf leaders have held a flurry of calls to ease tensions. Iran's nuclear programme remains the hardest issue in any deal.

facts.target: an air defence system on Qeshm Island

update.new: A second round of US strikes on Qeshm, and a $20m reward offer.
update.front: The US has struck Iran again days after voters punished Trump over the war.

seconds.headline: Trump makes Stephen Miller, who once called India's Russian oil purchases 'not acceptable', his chief of staff
seconds.short: Stephen Miller, the architect of Donald Trump's hardline immigration policies, has become White House chief of staff after Susie Wiles said she would step down following the Republicans' loss of Congress. Miller, 41, was deputy chief of staff. In 2025 he said India's purchases of Russian oil were "not acceptable" and accused India of "cheating" the US immigration system.

why.text: Miller has pushed for tougher H-1B rules and tariffs on India, and now runs the White House for Trump's last two years.

more: Miller claimed in 2025 that India was tied with China in buying Russian crude, helping to "finance" the war in Ukraine, and accused India of "massive tariffs" on American goods; the US went on to put a 25% tariff on Indian products. He has also pushed to restrict skilled foreign workers and tighten H-1B visa rules. He has, though, called the Trump-Modi friendship "a tremendous relationship with India".

Earlier this year Miller called Alex Pretti, a US citizen shot dead by a Border Patrol agent in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist", before saying the agents "may not have been following" protocol. Indian-American voters, who had warmed to Republicans in 2024, swung to Democrats this time.

update.new: Trump's first big change after the defeat: Miller as chief of staff.
update.front: Trump answers the midterm defeat by putting his hardest-line adviser in charge.

seconds.headline: Alcaraz saves two match points to beat Fritz and reach his first Paris Masters semi-final, against Ruud tonight
seconds.short: Carlos Alcaraz saved two match points to beat Taylor Fritz 6-7, 7-5, 6-3 in the Paris Masters quarter-finals on Friday, reaching the semi-finals for the first time. He plays Casper Ruud on Court Central at 21:30 IST tonight. "Probably this match is going to be one of the most special matches that I ever played," he said.

why.text: He is two wins from the only big indoor title he has not won, a week before the ATP Finals.

more: Alcaraz lost a first-set tiebreak in which both men had set points. Fritz broke in the seventh game of the second set; Alcaraz saved one match point with a backhand slice from well wide of his own tramlines and another with a passing shot, then broke back twice. "I started to smile; I started to bring the energy from the people to the match," he said.

The comeback recalled his win over Jannik Sinner in last year's French Open final, when he saved three championship points. Fritz's defeat knocked him out of the race for Turin and sent Rafael Jodar to the ATP Finals. Ruud beat the lucky loser Nuno Borges 7-6, 6-4.

update.new: He beat Fritz from two match points down; Ruud next.
update.front: Alcaraz is in a Paris semi-final for the first time, after one of his great escapes.

seconds.headline: The Sensex closes the week at 81,028 after its biggest weekly gain in six years, and the Nifty passes 25,000
seconds.short: The Sensex rose 2.2% on Friday to close at 81,028, adding another 637 points after Friday's 14:00 paper, and the Nifty 50 closed above 25,000 for the first time since 27 February. It was the indices' biggest weekly gain in six years, and a 10.6% rise in seven sessions before Diwali, the best such run in 35 years.

why.text: Cheaper oil and returning foreign money have lifted Indian shares even as US tech stocks crashed, and that helps every Indian saver's portfolio.

more: Mahindra & Mahindra, ICICI Bank and HDFC Life led the Nifty on Friday, and private banks did best among sectors, as money moved out of the global AI trade. Smaller companies lagged: the Nifty SmallCap 100 fell 0.8% and the MidCap 100 was flat. The Nifty's close was its best since the West Asia war began.

Foreign investors bought nearly ₹15,000 crore of Indian shares on Thursday alone. Brent crude is near $98 a barrel after falling about 9% on Wednesday, and the rupee has firmed to about 93.9 a dollar. Markets are shut for the weekend; Diwali is on Sunday.

update.new: Friday's close: the best week in six years.
update.front: Indian shares have had their best pre-Diwali run in 35 years.

seconds.headline: Paraguay's Senate impeaches Santiago Peña instead of accepting his resignation, and he is put under house arrest
seconds.short: Paraguay's Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest on Friday, minutes after senators voted 44 to 0 to remove him over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has left more than half the population unable to reach their savings. Rather than accept his resignation, they charged him with misconduct, stripping the immunity former presidents usually enjoy.

why.text: A president jailed over a bank he once part-owned is a rare, stark reckoning for a regulatory failure.

more: The charges allege conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds and an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña, who held shares in the bank's parent company until last year, denies wrongdoing. Prosecutor Silvia Margarita González Vester said he will be questioned on Saturday over breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds.

Vice-president Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim president until 2028 and promised that people hit by the collapse would be "fully compensated". About 3 million depositors still cannot reach their savings and pensions; police used tear gas and water cannon at earlier protests.

update.front: A sitting president has gone from resignation to house arrest in a day.

stories.headline: Sonia Gandhi says 12 years of BJP rule have done 'great damage' to India's institutions, and defends the Emergency as constitutional
stories.byline: THE HINDU · THE TIMES OF INDIA · 7 NOV
stories.short: Sonia Gandhi told The Hindu in a rare interview that "over the last twelve years, great damage has been done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions". She said repairing them will take time even after the BJP leaves office. On the 1975 Emergency, she said rights were curtailed but it was done constitutionally.

why.text: It is a rare long interview from the Congress's most senior figure, days after the party's biggest rally in years.

more: "People are now beginning to be restless and recognising the damage. But I am optimistic, and I know that the people of India will welcome a return to proper governance," she said. Restoring the systems would need "great effort from political parties", she added.

On the Emergency, she said: "Yes, democratic rights had been curtailed, and there was a suspension of habeas corpus, but it was done constitutionally." Seeing it from Indira Gandhi's point of view, she said, she saw her "struggling to cope" with violent protests, burning government offices and public transport, and calls for the bureaucracy and armed forces to disobey orders. She said she understood the gravity of that period only after it ended.

stories.headline: Gurnoor Brar's four wickets bowl New Zealand out for 134 in Wellington, and Kohli passes Ponting's record against them
stories.byline: THE TIMES OF INDIA · ESPNCRICINFO · 7 NOV
stories.short: India bowled New Zealand out for 134 in 41 overs in the rain-shortened second ODI in Wellington on Saturday, with Gurnoor Brar taking four wickets. Virat Kohli's first-ball boundary made him the highest ODI run-scorer against New Zealand, passing Ricky Ponting's 1,971, but he fell for seven. India were 89 for five after 21 overs at the cut.

why.text: A win would put India 2-0 up in the five-match series with three games to go.

more: Persistent rain delayed the toss and cut the match to 47 overs a side, and India chose to bowl with an unchanged side. Brar used short balls to remove Tom Latham and Glenn Phillips, while Auqib Nabi, Anshul Kamboj and Axar Patel took two wickets each.

Kohli, 37, now has 1,975 ODI runs against New Zealand, ahead of Ponting, Sachin Tendulkar's 1,750 and Kumar Sangakkara's 1,568. He made 74 in the first ODI in Auckland as India chased a revised target of 143 under the DLS method. At the cut India needed 46 more runs with five wickets left. The third ODI is in Hamilton on Tuesday.

update.new: The second ODI: New Zealand 134 all out, India chasing.

stories.headline: An 11-year-old boy who survived the Rajajinagar killings says the accused drove him around while throwing bags from the car
stories.short: An 11-year-old boy rescued when police arrested Indushekar, accused of killing seven of his family in Rajajinagar, says the man told him they were going on a trip and kept throwing big plastic bags out of the car. Police say the bags probably held the bodies of the boy's parents, and suspect the boy was the next target.

why.text: The boy's account shows how close the death toll came to eight, and helps police find the remaining bodies.

more: "Whenever I asked about my parents, he diverted the topic and told me that we were going on a trip," the boy said. "When I tried to open the boot of the car to check what he was doing, he scolded me." Police believe the accused drove with the bodies in the boot and the boy inside.

The boy said Indushekar took him first to the airport and then to Kukke Subrahmanya, Dharmasthala and Sringeri. His family had come to a dinner at the accused's house on 31 October and were made to stay late; they told their landlords to keep the gate open, but never returned. Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said the boy "was the next target".

update.new: A boy survived, and says the accused drove him around with the bodies.
